title: On-call and Incident Response Playbook — Process, Runbooks, Postmortems & Templates
author: Priya Nair
body:
Overview:

This playbook defines Redwood Inference’s on-call and incident response practices: severity definitions, responsibilities, runbook templates, postmortem process, rotation guidance, game-day exercises, and status page / customer communications templates. It is intended for on-call engineers, incident commanders (ICs), SREs, support, and engineering managers.

Key goals:
- Restore service quickly and safely while protecting customer data and minimizing user impact.
- Triage and remediate incidents with clear roles and escalation paths.
- Capture learnings via consistent postmortems and corrective actions.
- Maintain a predictable on-call rotation and healthy on-call practices.

Table of contents:
1) Incident lifecycle and severity definitions
2) Roles & responsibilities
3) On-call rotations and handoffs
4) Runbook templates and sample runbooks
5) Postmortem process and template
6) Game day checklist and running exercises
7) Status page and customer comms templates
8) Appendices: SLOs, alert thresholds, tooling links

1) Incident lifecycle and severity definitions

- Detection: Alerts from monitoring (Prometheus/Alertmanager), customer reports, or automated health checks.
- Triage: On-call responder acknowledges and determines severity.
- Containment: Actions to limit blast radius (traffic reroute, scale up, config rollback).
- Remediation: Apply a fix or mitigation.
- Recovery: Restore full service and validate.
- Review: Runbook updates and postmortem.

Severity levels (use these labels in PagerDuty and internal comms):
- sev-1 / P0 (Critical): Customer-facing outage affecting >5% of production traffic or severe data loss risk. Target: page immediately, IC engages within 5 minutes.
- sev-2 / P1 (High): Significant degradation (latency/throughput) impacting important customers or features. Page on-call and notify IC within 15 minutes.
- sev-3 / P2 (Medium): Partial degradation, reduced functionality for a subset of users. Triage within 1 hour.
- sev-4 / P3 (Low): Non-urgent issues, scheduled work, or informational alerts. Handle during business hours.

2) Roles & responsibilities

- Primary on-call (Responder): Acknowledges alerts, does first-line triage, runs runbooks, and escalates.
- Incident Commander (IC): Coordinates cross-team activity, communicates status, assigns tasks, and owns the incident timeline and severity decisions.
- Subject Matter Expert (SME): Service owners, SREs, or infra engineers who implement root fixes.
- Communications Lead: Owns status page updates and customer-facing messages.
- Postmortem author: Usually the IC or an assigned engineer; responsible for documenting timeline, impact, and action items.

Escalation matrix (example):
1. Primary on-call -> 15 minutes -> Escalate to Secondary on-call / team lead
2. 30 minutes unresolved or customer impact increases -> Page IC and Eng Manager
3. 60 minutes unresolved with ongoing customer impact -> Exec escalation (on-call director), legal/PR notified if required

3) On-call rotations and handoffs

- Rotation cadence: 1 week primary on-call shifts to balance continuity and burnout. Secondary rotation runs in parallel for coverage.
- Handoff procedure (required at shift change):
  1) Outgoing sends a short status summary in #oncall-status: current incidents, mitigations, pager notes, ongoing work, blocked items.
  2) Incoming ACKs and asks clarifying questions.
  3) Update PagerDuty escalation policies if temporary overrides were applied.
- Time off & swap policy: Engineers should coordinate swaps at least 48 hours in advance via the on-call scheduling tool and notify team Slack channel. Emergency swaps use the rotation manager or SRE lead.
- On-call best practices:
  - Keep runbooks updated after every incident.
  - Use quiet hours sparingly; ensure backup coverage if using.
  - Avoid long-running tasks that risk distracted responders while on-call.

4) Runbook templates and sample runbooks

Runbook template (use for all critical services):
- Title: short service/runbook name
- Owner: service owner and pager alias
- Impact: what user-visible symptoms look like
- Detection methods: alerts, dashboards, health checks
- Immediate checks (quick triage checklist):
  - Check recent deploys (git commit / CI pipeline)
  - Verify upstream/downstream dependencies
  - Check for infrastructure changes (autoscaling, networking, certificates)
  - Look at 5xx rates, latency (p50/p95/p99), queue lengths
- Mitigation steps (ordered, safe to run):
  1) Identify and switch traffic to fallback region / standby model if available.
  2) Temporarily increase replicas / capacity.
  3) Apply rate-limiting or circuit-breaker to reduce load.
  4) Rollback recent deploy to previous stable revision.
- Remediation steps: list root fixes with pointers to PRs and owner.
- Post-incident actions: timeline, tags, changed configs, and required postmortem.
- Runbook last-updated: date and author

Sample runbook: API gateway high 5xx rate
- Title: api-gateway-high-5xx
- Owner: api-platform-oncall (pager: pd-api-oncall)
- Impact: Increased 5xx responses from gateway; clients observe errors for request paths /v1/generate and /v1/embeddings.
- Detection: Alert: gateway_5xx_rate > 1% for 5m; Dashboard: p95 latency > 600ms.
- Immediate checks:
  1) Confirm recent deploys: curl -s https://ci.internal/api/latest-deploys | jq .
  2) Check upstream service (model-serving) 5xx and evictions.
  3) Inspect gateway logs: kubectl logs -n api deployment/gateway -c proxy --tail=200 | grep ERROR
- Mitigation (ordered):
  1) Enable safe-mode traffic policy: route 100% traffic to stable pool (ctrl-plane CLI: rctl route set --service api-gateway --pool stable).
  2) Scale gateway replicas: kubectl scale deploy/gateway --replicas=6 -n api
  3) If surge is due to a model, blacklist offending model variant in routing table.
  4) If due to a bad deploy, rollback: kubectl rollout undo deployment/gateway -n api --to-revision=<previous>
- Remediation: Create a fix PR pinned to owner, link to issue tracker (e.g., JIRA-1234).
- Post-incident: Run the postmortem template within 48 hours.

5) Postmortem process and template

When to run a postmortem:
- Any sev-1 incident must have a postmortem published within 72 hours.
- Sev-2 incidents require a postmortem if customer-facing SLA was violated or root cause is unclear.

Postmortem template (publish to /confluence/incident-postmortems):
- Title: incident-YYYYMMDD-short-description
- Author: incident commander / assigned author
- Severity: sev-1|sev-2|...
- Summary (1-2 sentences)
- Timeline (chronological, timestamps in UTC)
- Impact: number of affected customers, duration, SLO violations, revenue/latency impact
- Root cause: concise technical cause, contributing factors, and human/process causes
- Detection & response: how was this detected, timeline of actions taken
- Corrective actions: concrete action items, owner, and due date (must be actionable and small)
- Preventative measures: longer-term engineering changes or process updates with owners
- Postmortem review: reviewers and approvals

Postmortem grading and follow-up:
- Each corrective action must be tracked in the issue tracker and linked to the postmortem.
- Engineering manager verifies completion within SLA (30 days for high priority items).
- Quarterly incident review to surface trends and common failure modes.

6) Game days and exercises

Purpose: validate runbooks, test tooling (alerting, on-call routing, status page), and practice cross-team coordination.

Game day planning checklist:
- Define scenario and success criteria.
- Schedule a 2-hour window with minimum disruption (use staging/blue environments).
- Invite on-call engineers, SREs, product owner, support, and communications lead.
- Prepare a post-exercise retro and update runbooks within 7 days.

Example exercises:
- Simulate control-plane outage: verify automated failover and fallback routing.
- Simulate increased model latency: validate cache and batching mitigations.
- Simulate customer-reported data integrity incident: test access controls and legal/PR communication steps.

7) Status page and customer communications templates

Status page update cadence during incidents:
- Initial update within 15 minutes for sev-1/2 incidents with: symptom summary, scopes affected, and estimated next update time.
- Follow-ups every 30 minutes for ongoing sev-1s until recovery.
- Final post-incident update when service restored with link to postmortem.

Status page template (short):
- Title: Service degradation — API Gateway (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC)
- Summary: We are seeing elevated 5xx rates on the API Gateway causing failed requests for some customers. Engineers are investigating.
- Impact: A subset of requests to /v1/* are returning 5xx errors.
- Scope: Customers in us-west-2 and eu-west-1 regions.
- Current status: Investigating / Mitigating / Identified / Monitoring / Resolved
- Next update: in 30 minutes

Customer-facing email/SaaS notice template:
- Subject: Incident report: degraded API availability (YYYY-MM-DD)
- Body:
  Hello <CustomerName>,

  We are writing to let you know about an incident that affected Redwood Inference’s API on <date/time UTC>.

  Summary: <one-line summary of impact>.

  What happened: <high-level cause — e.g., configuration error in gateway>.

  Impact: <which endpoints, percent of requests, customers affected>.

  What we did: <mitigations and timeline>.

  Next steps: <postmortem link, corrective actions, contact>.

  We apologize for the disruption. If you have questions about this incident, please contact your account team or support@redwood.ai.

  Sincerely,
  Redwood Inference Operations Team

Internal comms template (Slack update):
- #incident-{id} pinned message:
  - Short summary, severity, IC, primary owner, and current action items.
  - Links to runbook, logs, and PagerDuty incident page.

8) Appendices: SLOs, alert thresholds, tooling links

SLO examples (service-level examples):
- API availability SLO: 99.9% availability over 30 days (measured excluding planned maintenance).
- Latency SLO: p95 < 250ms for /v1/generate; p99 < 800ms.
- Embeddings throughput SLO: mean batch latency < 200ms at expected load.

Alerting thresholds (examples):
- gateway_5xx_rate > 1% for 5 minutes -> sev-2 alert
- model_serving_evictions > 3 in 10m -> sev-1 alert
- cluster_node_cpu > 90% for 10m -> sev-2

Tooling & links:
- PagerDuty schedules & escalation: https://pagerduty.internal/teams/api-platform
- Status page management: https://status.redwood.ai
- Incident tracker template: https://jira.internal/browse/INCIDENT
- Runbook repository: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks
- Monitoring dashboards: https://grafana.internal/d/redwood

Appendix: quick CLI examples
- Check recent deploys: curl -s https://ci.internal/api/latest-deploys | jq .
- Tail gateway logs: kubectl -n api logs -l app=gateway --tail=200 -c proxy | grep ERROR
- Trigger safe-mode routing (control plane CLI): rctl route set --service api-gateway --pool stable

Review & governance:
- This playbook is reviewed annually and after every sev-1 incident.
- Runbooks must include a last-updated date and owner; teams failing to maintain runbooks will be flagged in quarterly reviews.

Contact & ownership:
- On-call policy owner: eng-sre team (eng-sre@redwood.ai)
- Playbook support: Priya Nair (pri@redwood.ai)
